messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Marcus is a 34-year-old married school counselor of North American background who presented for assessment following a significant decline in his occupational and personal functioning over the preceding eighteen months. His PCL-5 score of 77 places him in the severe range of posttraumatic symptomatology, and the picture that emerged across the intake and early sessions was one of a man whose sense of self had been fundamentally fractured by a single afternoon that he cannot fully leave behind.

Approximately two years ago, Marcus was driving home from work on a rainy evening when, momentarily distracted by his phone, he struck a cyclist who had moved into his lane. The impact was violent. He remembers stepping out of the car and smelling the rain mixed with something metallic — blood and asphalt — and kneeling beside the cyclist, a teenager, whose injuries were severe. Emergency services arrived within minutes, but Marcus remained on the scene, hands shaking, unable to form complete sentences when the paramedics questioned him. The teenager survived but sustained lasting physical damage. No criminal charges were filed, but that legal resolution did nothing to quiet what Marcus had already decided about himself: that he had done this, that it was entirely his fault, and that a person capable of such carelessness could not be trusted.

In the weeks that followed, Marcus began to notice that certain things pulled him back to the road. The smell of rain on warm pavement — something he encountered every morning walking from the school parking lot — could stop him mid-step, his chest tightening, his body flooding with the physical reactivity that had no regard for whether he was standing in a hallway full of teenagers or sitting in his own kitchen. When those sensory cues arrived, the memory did not feel like a recollection; it felt like a resumption, as though the accident were still unfolding across all his senses simultaneously, vivid and immediate and inescapable. He found himself unable to describe what had happened to his wife in any coherent way — he knew the sequence of events, but the words dissolved before he could speak them, leaving him silent and ashamed in a way that deepened his conviction that something essential in him had broken.

His appraisals of himself hardened over time into something close to certainty. He had come to believe that the event had happened because of the way he acted — the phone, the split second of inattention — and that this was not an aberration but a revelation of who he truly was. He was certain he could not trust himself to do the right thing in any high-stakes moment, a belief that made his work as a school counselor quietly unbearable. When a student arrived in crisis, Marcus would feel the familiar surge of fear and guilt, and the thought that he might fail this child the way he had failed the cyclist would trigger the memory all over again, pulling him back to the smell and the sound and the teenager on the wet road. The belief that his life had been destroyed by the trauma was not metaphorical to Marcus; it was a daily accounting of everything he could no longer be.

To manage this, Marcus had constructed an elaborate architecture of avoidance. He kept his mind occupied at all times — podcasts during his commute, administrative tasks stacked deliberately to crowd out any reflective space, television running through the evening. He avoided thinking about the event directly and had rerouted his driving routes to avoid passing police vehicles, which brought the scene rushing back with a physical force that left him sweating and hyperalert. Yet these strategies had begun to work against him. The constant mental occupation prevented him from processing anything, and the suppression itself seemed to make the memory more intrusive, surfacing with greater vividness precisely when he had been most vigilant against it. The avoidance had also eroded his marriage; his wife described him as absent even when present, and he had declined a medical check-up twice, unable to tolerate the clinical smells of a doctor's office. He slept poorly, lying awake in a state of low-level alertness he could not explain or switch off.

What finally brought Marcus to seek help was a session with a student in which he had frozen entirely — unable to respond, flooded, staring at the wall — and the student had gone to find another adult. He arrived at intake frightened that he was becoming a danger to the young people he was supposed to protect, and most hoping, he said quietly, that someone could help him believe the accident was something that happened to him, rather than proof of everything he feared he was.
